content:
A student once asked me why 1/8 is 0.125 but 1/3 ‘refuses to end’. Good question, and the SAT is built on it. Some fractions turn into clean decimals, and some run forever. Knowing which is which saves you real seconds under the clock. This free SAT Math Fractions and Decimals practice test online gives you 15 MCQs to build that fluency, with instant answers below. Speed here quietly lifts your whole Math score, because almost every other chapter leans on it.

What the SAT expects with fractions and decimals

The exam rarely asks for a plain calculation. Instead it buries fractions inside rates, ratios and data. So the four operations must be automatic, not slow. And decimals must feel like fractions in disguise. Here is the ground the chapter covers:

  • Adding and subtracting with a common denominator.
  • Multiplying straight across, then simplifying.
  • Dividing by flipping the second fraction and multiplying.
  • Converting between fractions, decimals and percents.
  • Comparing and ordering values quickly.

Three moves behind the SAT Math Fractions and Decimals practice test online

Most students do not need new rules. They need cleaner habits. First, memorise the common families. The eighths give 0.125, 0.25, 0.375 and so on, and the thirds give repeating decimals. Then a conversion takes no thought. Second, never divide by a fraction directly. Flip it and multiply, every single time. Third, simplify before you multiply, not after. That keeps the numbers small and the errors rare.

The questionWeak moveStrong move
Divide 3/4 by 2/5Divide top and bottom separatelyFlip to 3/4 × 5/2 = 15/8
Which is larger, 5/8 or 0.6?Guess from the digits5/8 = 0.625, so 5/8 wins
Add 2/3 + 1/6Add tops and bottomsUse sixths: 4/6 + 1/6 = 5/6

Why ‘flip and multiply’ is non-negotiable

Division by a fraction trips up strong students under pressure. So make it mechanical. Dividing by 2/5 is the same as multiplying by 5/2. The rule never changes, so you never have to think about it. Practise it until your hand does it for you. That freed-up attention is exactly what harder questions demand.

A trap the SAT loves

Ordering mixed forms is the classic snare. A list might read 3/5, 0.58 and 62%. Students compare them in three different formats and slip. So convert everything to decimals first. Then 3/5 is 0.6, and the order is clear. Here is the counter-intuitive part: the slow-looking step of converting first is actually the fast route to the right answer.

Why fluency here pays off everywhere

Here is the part students underrate. Fractions and decimals look like the warm-up chapter, yet they feed the hard ones. Ratios need clean fraction sense. Percent problems are just fractions in another coat. Slopes, rates and probability all rest on the same skill. So the minutes you spend here come back across the whole section. In my experience coaching SAT students, the ones who drill conversions early stop losing marks to silly arithmetic. And fewer silly errors, not fancy tricks, is what nudges a 640 toward 740.

A quick worked example

Suppose you need 2/3 of 45, then a further 40% off the result. Take two clean steps. First, 2/3 of 45 is 30. Then a 40% cut leaves 60%, so multiply 30 by 0.6 to get 18. Notice the rhythm: one operation at a time, simplify as you go. The SAT rewards that patience far more than clever shortcuts.
